methodological_rigor.justification: Retrospective multicenter subgroup analysis of the WJOG15421L/REVEAL study (n=1479 analyzed, 229 post-operative recurrence subgroup) across 29 institutions. Univariate and multivariate logistic regression with backward stepwise selection identifies predictors of multigene testing. Kaplan-Meier survival analysis with Cox proportional hazards reports HRs and 95% CIs. Authors acknowledge selection bias and non-consecutive enrollment. Sample size of 229 limits power for subgroup analyses; no formal correction for multiple comparisons reported. Survival analyses compare post-operative recurrence vs advanced cohorts which differ systematically beyond treatment group.

clinical_relevance_loe.justification: Retrospective observational cohort study with prospective follow-up from a multicenter registry - Oxford LoE 2b. Clinical relevance is high: identifies under-utilization of multigene testing (43.7%) in post-operative NSCLC recurrence with actionable predictors (nonadenocarcinoma histology, >3 years from surgery). Directly relevant to current perioperative NSCLC care in the era of adjuvant osimertinib and atezolizumab, informing clinical guideline implementation and quality improvement.

reporting_quality.justification: Authors explicitly state adherence to STROBE guidelines; study registered in UMIN (UMIN000046079); ethical approval (Tottori University Faculty of Medicine central review board) and written informed consent documented. Patient flow described (1500 enrolled, 21 excluded, 229 subgroup, 1 excluded). Specific Python package versions reported (pandas 1.5.3, NumPy 1.24.2, SciPy 1.10.0, statsmodels 0.13.5, lifelines 0.27.4). Tables present demographics and univariate/multivariate results clearly. Data availability beyond supplementary tables is not discussed.

novelty_literature.justification: Authors claim this is the first study specifically examining biomarker testing status in post-operative NSCLC recurrence. Meaningful extension of prior testing-rate literature (e.g., Sakamoto et al. 2023 JAMA Network Open) to the post-operative recurrence population. Findings are descriptive and confirmatory more than conceptually novel; the survival difference between post-operative recurrence and advanced cases is consistent with prior reports. Useful quality-improvement/health services finding but not paradigm-shifting.

writing_presentation.justification: Well-organized manuscript with clear Introduction-Methods-Results-Discussion-Conclusions structure. Tables and figures support key findings effectively. Bullet-point key findings at start enhance reader accessibility. Discussion appropriately contextualizes results with limitations (selection bias, variable test timing, specialized-center bias) and contemporary perioperative therapy advances (osimertinib, atezolizumab, nivolumab+chemotherapy).

key_strengths: First dedicated analysis of multigene testing status and prognosis in post-operative recurrent NSCLC from a large multicenter Japanese cohort
Identifies actionable predictors: nonadenocarcinoma histology (adjusted OR 0.40) and time from surgery >3 years (adjusted OR 0.43) associated with lower testing rates
STROBE-adherent reporting with explicit trial registration (UMIN000046079) and open software version reporting
Survival comparisons between post-operative recurrence and advanced cohorts with driver-positive/negative stratification
key_concerns: Subgroup sample size (n=229) limits statistical power for stratified analyses
Retrospective observational design with acknowledged selection bias (non-consecutive enrollment) and potential timing bias in biomarker testing
Generalizability limited: surveyed facilities are specialized cancer centers in Japan, may not represent broader practice
Cross-sectional snapshot (2020-2021); testing practice has likely evolved with introduction of newer panels
No multiple testing correction reported for the many subgroup comparisons
chief_reviewer.rationale: Competent observational subgroup analysis with clear clinical quality-improvement implications but incremental novelty and modest sample size, fitting Tier 3 (European Journal of Cancer / Clinical Lung Cancer-caliber) with minor revisions.
